newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO ready to set seal on infotech pact,trade agenda.
newsitem.headline: WTO ready to set seal on infotech pact,trade agenda.

text.p: Ministers from 128 nations prepared on Friday to put the seal on a sweeping pact to free up commerce in information technology and set the agenda of world trade talks for the rest of the century.

Delegates said only minor details had to be settled before a final declaration could be approved later in the day summing up the achievements of the first week-long ministerial meeting of the fledgling World Trade Organisation (WTO).

The last stumbling block was over language to mollify developing countries upset that rich nations had refused to back WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero's proposal to give the world's 48 poorest countries duty-free access for their exports.
The highlight of the conference was an accord to scrap tariffs on the rapidly growing $600 billion world market in computer-related goods.

Ministers and economists said the agreement would give a powerful boost to the information-technology (IT) industry, especially in Asia, and eventually lead to lower prices for a vast range of consumer goods that use electronic parts.

But delegates said the triumph of clinching an IT pact, which about 30 countries were expected to sign on Friday, would had been tarnished without agreement on the conference's other main agenda item -- the link between trade and labour standards.
A hard-fought compromise emerged late on Thursday that had just enough to enable North and South to proclaim victory.
"We got everything," said Ruggiero, tired but happy after days of round-the-clock negotiations.

Developing nations, led by India, Pakistan and Egypt, had refused to countenance any interference by the WTO in the area of workers' rights, fearing it would undermine their chief comparative advantage in world trade -- cheap labour.

The United States and a string of European countries, by contrast, were equally insistent in clamouring for action to help 250 million child workers, mainly in the Third World, and to improve sweatshop conditions.

The final declaration satisfies poor countries because it firmly rejects the use of labour standards for protectionist purposes and says the International Labour Organisation, based like the WTO in Geneva, is the competent body to deal with them.
"We are happy with what has come out," said Pakistan's commerce minister, Muhammad Zubair Khan.

Washington, however, can point to a commitment in the closing declaration to observe internationally recognised labour standards and to a promise of continued collaboration between the WTO and the ILO.
"If the Americans hadn't got an agreement on labour, they couldn't have gone back to Washington," a Japanese official said.

Diplomats said a clarifying statement from the conference chairman after the declaration is approved by a plenary session on Friday would make clear that the WTO would not carry out any follow-up work on labour.
But Washington has been fighting for higher worldwide labour standards for 40 years, and U.S. officials insist the issue will not simply go away -- regardless of the outcome this week.
"The Americans have already said no one can ever be stopped from raising anything in the WTO," said a developing country envoy.
Agreement on other items on the WTO's future work programme, including the link between trade and cross-border investment and competition policies, was reached earlier in ther week.
